ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, there is a rod AO of negligible mass, with length R, which can freely rotate about A. A object with weight G is suspended by a rope at point O, and one end of another rope is tied at point O, while the other end is tied at point C on the arc-shaped wall. During the process in which point C gradually moves upward along the arc CB from the position shown in the figure (keeping the angle $\theta$ between OA and the ground unchanged), the change in the magnitude of the tension in rope OC is (　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, there is a rod AO of negligible mass, with length R, which can freely rotate about A. A object with weight G is suspended by a rope at point O, and one end of another rope is tied at point O, while the other end is tied at point C on the arc-shaped wall. During the process in which point C gradually moves upward along the arc CB from the position shown in the figure (keeping the angle $\theta$ between OA and the ground unchanged), how does the magnitude of the tension in rope OC change?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, point A is at the bottom, and rod AO connects from A obliquely to the upper left to O; the angle between the rod and the ground is labeled θ; point O is also connected to a vertically downward rope, below which an object with weight G is suspended. Another rope connects from O obliquely to the right to point C on the arc-shaped wall, and the arc continues upward to point B. The meaning of the problem is that C moves upward along arc CB, while the direction of OA remains unchanged. Reasoning: At point O, it can be regarded as three-force equilibrium: the suspended object gives point O a downward tension of magnitude G through the vertical rope; rope OC gives point O a tension T_OC along OC, pointing toward C; the force of the massless rod AO on point O is along the direction of AO. Because θ remains unchanged, the direction of AO is fixed, and the direction of gravity is also fixed, therefore the component of G perpendicular to AO is a constant. Let the angle between OC and AO be φ. Writing equilibrium along the direction perpendicular to AO, there is T_OC sinφ = constant, so T_OC = constant / sinφ. It can be seen from the figure that, during the process in which C moves upward from the shown position along the arc to B, the direction of OC relative to AO first gradually approaches perpendicular, that is, sinφ first increases; after passing the position close to perpendicular, sinφ then decreases. Therefore T_OC first decreases as sinφ increases, and then increases as sinφ decreases.
